anyways here is the free prompt thank me later ↓

<inputs>
Ask me for my story, or pitch 3.
- A good one is true and little known. Someone does something that looks ridiculous, someone laughs at them, and the reveal flips who was smart: a trick, a scheme, a bluff, a loophole, revenge.
- Give each pitch with its first line, the mocker, the twist, and a title that hides the ending.
Ask which voice I want:
- Free, the default: Kokoro, run locally on the CPU.
- Optional upgrade: ElevenLabs with a stock library voice. Tell me the credit cost before you generate anything, and make one take.
Ask what GPU I have. Any GPU works: Blender EEVEE renders on all of them, just slower on older cards.
Tell me everything else is free: Blender, Python, Playwright with a headless browser, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, Pixabay music and Mixkit sound effects. No image, video or 3D model generator is used anywhere.
Then write the script and the beat list with seconds, and show me both before you build anything.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1080x1920, 30 fps, 55-70 s vertical Short in the style of narrated "true story with a twist" cartoon Shorts: flat 2D cartoon people acting inside lit, dressed 3D toon sets, one storyteller voice, captions of 1-2 words, and one camera that keeps travelling.

Sets (Blender, built by a Python script):
- Build every place in the story from simple shapes in code (boxes, cylinders, cones, tori, bevelled boxes), never a downloaded model.
- Materials: flat toon colours with low roughness, so it reads like a cartoon, not a photo.
- Ink outlines: an inverted-hull shell on every object (a Solidify modifier with flipped normals and a dark backface-only material), so the world has the same line as the characters.
- Draw surfaces on a canvas and use them as textures: signs, chalkboards, brick, planks, plaques.
- Put the story's words inside the world (signs, boards, counters) instead of floating titles.
Palette and light:
- Pick a warm key against cool shadows for each place. Balance cream, ochre and amber against blue, teal and purple.
- Costumes contrast with the set.
- Interiors: warm practical lamps plus a soft cool fill. Exteriors: a strong sun, a blue sky and a lighter horizon.
- Render with EEVEE, the Standard view transform, a slight lowered exposure, and a soft glow added in the finish.
People:
- 2D characters are drawn in code (HTML canvas) and exported as transparent images, one per pose and expression. In Blender they sit on camera-facing cards that turn around the vertical axis only.
- Use an emission material on the cards so faces stay clean white whatever the lighting.
- The look, kept simple:
  - a big round white head with a thick dark brush outline
  - big expressive eyes and brows, a small nose, a mouth that changes shape
  - thin stick legs and chunky flat-colour clothes
  - one signature prop or accessory each (glasses, a hat, a cigar, a tool)
- The face set: smug, grin, shock, laughing, worried, sweat drops.
- Pose-to-pose acting: point, hold up a prop, hands on hips, arms up. Blinks and small breathing keep holds alive.
- A new, original cast for every video. Show me a character sheet before building.
Camera:
- One camera that travels between beats. Each beat holds with a slow push, then the camera moves to the next.
- Fit every camera key to what it should show: compute the distance so the named faces or props sit fully in frame.
- Inserts carry the proof: a close-up on the key object while the change happens.
- The payoff is the biggest frame in the video: a reveal coming at the lens.
- Soft dissolves or camera moves between places, few hard cuts.
Captions:
- 1-2 words at a time; short words (a, the, so, to) ride with the next word.
- A bold rounded font, white with a thick dark outline, centred in the lower third.
- No full stops on screen.
Banned:
- AI images or video, downloaded 3D models, real logos
- a camera that sits still
- half-cut faces, legs-only or hat-only frames, empty backgrounds
- a time-stretched or whispered voice
- more than one or two names the viewer has to remember
</direction>

<structure>
Length: 55-70 s, about 150-200 words.
Beat map for a 62 s Short (scale it to your voice):
0-4 s, HOOK: one plain sentence about an act that makes no sense, with the reason hidden. Picture it in one frame.
4-12 s, SETUP: who, where, and what's at stake, with one exact number.
12-20 s, THE MOCKER: a quoted joke line said to the hero. Big close-up.
20-40 s, THE METHOD: it gets weirder in steps. One close-up insert per step.
40-50 s, "YOU SEE,": the trick explained through an everyday thing the viewer has done.
50-62 s, THE PAYOFF and THE TWIST: shown, not explained. The last line is the biggest reveal and calls back to the hook.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools (all free): Blender (any recent version), Python 3, Node with Playwright, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, numpy. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Script:
   - Tell it the way a kid tells a friend: plain words, sentences joined with "and" and "so", one funny comparison, no dates or jargon.
   - Join related sentences with commas, because a voice resets after every full stop and leaves a gap.
   - Show me the word count and the seconds per line.
3. Voice:
   - Free route: Kokoro on the CPU, one line per call, joined with short gaps.
   - Paid route: ElevenLabs, one take, cost stated first.
   - Only trim silence, never inside a word. Then run faster-whisper on the finished track to get word times.
4. Characters: draw the cast in code, show me a sheet, then export every pose/expression the story needs as transparent WebP.
5. Story timeline: one file that, for any frame, returns the camera (position, look-at, fov, roll), the focus distance, and each character's card, position and scale. Anchor every beat and sound to a word time, never a typed time.
6. Exporter: a headless browser page runs the timeline for every frame and writes frames.json plus the card images and sign textures.
7. Blender scene script (blender -b -P http://scene.py -- --data data --out frames):
   - builds every set, light and prop
   - reads frames.json, places the camera and cards each frame, animates the props
   - renders JPG frames, skips frames that already exist so it can resume
8. Contact sheet before the full render: stills from the middle of every shot, labelled with time and the line being spoken. I approve or ask for changes.
9. Sound:
   - Music: one playful bed under a free licence, about 20 dB under the voice.
   - Effects: real Mixkit sounds placed on the actions (whooshes on camera travels, pops on reveals, impacts, dings).
   - Duck music and effects under speech. Normalise to -14 LUFS.
10. Finish with FFmpeg: a soft glow (screen-blend a blurred highlight pass at about 0.4 opacity), burned-in captions, the mix, H.264.
11. Give me a one-click .bat (or .sh) that runs the export, the Blender render and the finish. It must refuse to encode if any frame is missing, and never overwrite an older video.
12. Upload text:
   - Title: "The [thing] That [strange act]", hiding the ending.
   - Cover: a clean frame of the payoff with no text.
</build>

<gotchas>
Script:
- Scripts that read like writing (names, dates, context, the twist in the hook) fall flat. Line 1 is the strange act with the reason hidden.
Voice:
- Short full-stop sentences make the voice stop-start. Join lines with commas.
- Trimming at whisper timestamps clips words. Trim on silence only, with a small guard.
Look:
- Empty sets read as cheap. Dress every place with props and background detail.
- Characters scaled too small look like kids next to tables. Scale them so they stand about 1.9 m against the real-size sets.
Camera:
- Hand-placed cameras crop faces at 9:16; the frame is narrow. Fit keys to the subjects and scan every frame for cut faces before rendering.
- A camera that flies through a wall, a canopy or a post reads as a glitch. Pick another angle or cut.
Render:
- 3D props attached to a 2D card must follow the card's turn, or they drift off the drawn body.
- A render that stops early (sleep, crash) must not be encoded into a short video. Check the frame count first.
- Turn off PC sleep before a long render.
Sound:
- Music only a few dB under the voice makes the narrator hard to hear. Keep it low and measure.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my story, or pitch 3. Then show me the script (word count and seconds per line) and the beat list before any voice is generated or any scene is built.
</start>

2119052238715019425.texto:
F*CKING GENIUS...

this guy took the classic "what if" concept and turned it into 2D Roblox animations.

his VERY FIRST video pulled 1.3M views, and he already monetized the entire channel.

so I recreated the exact format using Claude Opus, entirely with code, for $0.

and I'm dropping the full prompt for FREE.

barely anyone is doing this format right now.

thank me later for this 👇

<ROLE>

You are my AI animation studio, Roblox animation director, scriptwriter, character designer, motion graphics engineer, and video production specialist.

Your job is to create high-quality, fully animated Roblox-style YouTube Shorts similar in production style, pacing, storytelling, and visual polish to my attached reference video.

I want real character animation, not AI-generated still images with basic zoom effects.

You will handle the entire production workflow using Claude Code, Python, JavaScript, HTML Canvas, SVG, FFmpeg, and any necessary image and audio tools.

Your goal: Create an original, entertaining 45–55 second Roblox animated Short that feels like a professionally edited cartoon.

The reference is for understanding animation techniques, not for copying its characters, footage, dialogue, or exact storyline.

Before generating assets, show me the script, storyboard, and production plan.

Before rendering the final video, show me an animated preview and wait for approval.

<STEP 1 — ANALYZE MY REFERENCE VIDEO>

First, inspect the MP4 file I attached.

Use FFprobe to identify:

Resolution

Frame rate
Duration
Audio streams
Video encoding
Extract frames at regular intervals, plus additional frames around major scene changes.

Create a contact sheet showing the entire video.

Analyze:

Character design

Background illustration style
Facial expressions
Character movement
Scene composition
Camera movements
Transitions
Subtitle placement
Subtitle animation
Color grading
Gaming HUD elements
Storytelling rhythm
Average scene duration
Sound effects and narration timing
If speech transcription is available, transcribe the narration and estimate the words spoken per minute.

Do not assume the narration from the subtitles alone.

REFERENCE CHARACTERISTICS

The reference runs approximately 50 seconds at 1080×1920 and 60 FPS.

It features:

2D blocky Roblox-inspired cartoon characters

Clean dark outlines around characters and objects
Simple geometric bodies
Large square or rounded-square heads
Exaggerated expressions
Bright, saturated colors
Stylized Roblox game worlds
Cartoon bedroom environments
Oversized virtual-game interfaces
A persistent countdown timer
Dramatic close-ups
Comedic reactions
Fast-paced editing
Animated word-by-word captions
The storytelling alternates between a real-world family situation and increasingly ridiculous events inside a virtual Roblox-style world.

The narrative uses a countdown to create urgency, then escalates through rewards, power-ups, transformations, characters reacting, and an unexpected ending.

Identify the specific techniques that make these sequences engaging.

Recreate those techniques using original assets.

<STEP 2 — ASK ME FOR MY STORY>

Before production, ask me:

1. What should the video be about?

Examples:

What If Dad Deleted Your Roblox Account?

What If You Had Unlimited Robux for 10 Seconds?

What If Every Roblox Game Combined Into One?
What If You Became the Richest Noob?
What If Your Roblox Character Could Talk?
What If You Had One Minute to Escape Roblox?
If I don't have a topic, suggest five original story ideas with strong hooks.
2. Which voice generation tool should we use?

Options:

ElevenLabs

Kokoro

Other available text-to-speech service
3. Which asset generation tools are available?
Options:

GPT Image

Another reference-capable image model

Fully programmatic SVG/vector illustration
Prefer code-generated reusable vector assets for elements requiring consistent animation.
Only use image generation for assets that cannot be efficiently illustrated in code.

Do not begin production until I approve the concept.

<STEP 3 — SCRIPT STRUCTURE>

Write an original 45–55 second script.

Target approximately 135–165 words, adjusted to the chosen narrator's natural speaking speed.

The storytelling must feel fast, funny, and unpredictable.

Use short sentences.

Make every sentence introduce an action, joke, reveal, or consequence.

Avoid lengthy explanations.

STORY FORMULA

0–3 seconds — THE HOOK

Open with an absurd Roblox-related situation.

Example:

"What if your dad gave you just TEN seconds to become the richest player in Roblox?"

Show the situation immediately.

No intro sequence.

No logos.

No slow setup.

3–8 seconds — THE RULES

Introduce the challenge or restriction.

Show the protagonist reacting.

Use an animated timer, warning, or game mechanic to create urgency.

8–15 seconds — THE FIRST WIN

The main character starts making progress.

Show an entertaining action sequence.

Introduce the first reward, achievement, or surprise.

15–24 seconds — ESCALATION

Increase the stakes.

Add something visually ridiculous:

Massive rewards

A difficult obstacle course

A giant enemy

A strange transformation
An unexpected purchase
A character gaining an absurd ability
Each new event should be more surprising than the previous one.
24–33 seconds — THE TWIST
Introduce an unexpected problem.

The protagonist's advantage creates a new challenge.

Use exaggerated character reactions.

33–43 seconds — COUNTDOWN AND PANIC

Increase the urgency.

Show the character trying to solve the problem.

Use faster cuts, close-ups, ticking sounds, and a changing timer.

43–50 seconds — COMEDIC PAYOFF

Deliver an unexpected outcome that connects to the opening situation.

50–55 seconds — LOOPABLE ENDING

End with a funny final line, cliffhanger, or question.

Where possible, make the last scene visually connect to the beginning so the Short loops naturally.

SCRIPT REQUIREMENTS

Every line must be visually actionable.

Do not write narration that cannot be shown through animation.

The protagonist should have a clear objective.

The story needs at least one surprise and one comedic payoff.

Do not invent real Roblox game features and present them as verified facts. Fictional powers and game mechanics are allowed when clearly part of the story.

Provide the complete script for approval.

<STEP 4 — VISUAL STYLE>

VIDEO SETTINGS

Resolution: 1080×1920

Aspect ratio: 9:16

Frame rate: 60 FPS

Format: MP4

Target duration: 45–55 seconds

ART DIRECTION

Create an original Roblox-inspired 2D cartoon universe.

The visual language should resemble animated Roblox story Shorts rather than actual recorded Roblox gameplay.

Use:

Blocky geometric bodies

Square and rounded-square heads

Large expressive eyes

Thick clean character outlines

Flat colors with simple highlights
Soft shadows
Colorful cartoon environments
Stylized lighting
Recognizable game-inspired objects
Oversized reaction expressions
Characters should look like designed cartoon avatars, not realistic humans.
Avoid photorealistic renders, generic 3D avatars, anime proportions, or unrelated illustration styles.
SUGGESTED PALETTE
Nighttime bedroom:

Dark navy: #111940

Deep purple: #24225B

Warm interior light: #F2C786

Teal accents: #20BDBB

Game world:
Sky blue: #80CDF5
Bright grass: #65C75A
Orange: #FF8528

Yellow: #FFD447

Pink: #FF5B9B
Gaming interface:
Dark charcoal: #222331
Success green: #30CE65
Warning red: #EE384A

Gold: #FFC83D

White: #FFFFFF
Use these as starting colors and refine them against the reference.
Maintain consistent lighting and colors within each environment.
<STEP 5 — CHARACTER SYSTEM>
Create a consistent original cast.

MAIN CHARACTER

A blocky Roblox-inspired avatar.

Design requirements:

Large square head

Recognizable hairstyle

Bold outfit color

Simple block torso

Rectangular arms

Short blocky legs
Large cartoon eyes
Expressive eyebrows
Animated mouth
The character's appearance must remain identical in every scene.
PARENT CHARACTER
Create a distinctive adult cartoon avatar.
Use different hair, clothing, silhouette, and facial features.
The parent should be able to show anger, confusion, excitement, surprise, and disbelief.

SIDE CHARACTERS

Generate additional original avatars as required by the script.

Each side character should be recognizable by silhouette and color.

CHARACTER SHEETS

Generate or draw each character in:

Front view

Side view

Three-quarter view

Back view

Idle pose

Running pose
Jumping pose
Surprised pose
Angry pose
Happy pose
Scared pose
Celebrating pose
Do not regenerate the entire character for every scene.
Create reusable layered assets and rigs.
CHARACTER RIGGING
Separate:
Head

Torso

Left arm

Right arm

Left hand

Right hand
Left leg
Right leg
Hair or accessories
Eyes
Eyebrows
Mouth
Maintain stable pivot points.
Store the rig configuration in a reusable data structure.
Animations should move the actual body parts rather than only translating a flattened character image.
<STEP 6 — FACIAL ANIMATION>
The characters must be expressive.

Create reusable facial expressions:

Neutral

Smiling

Excited

Surprised

Angry

Sad

Crying
Terrified
Confused
Smug
Screaming
Laughing
EYES
Animate blinking approximately every 2.5–4 seconds with slight timing variation.
Allow eyes to widen during surprises.
Use eye position changes to communicate attention.
EYEBROWS
Animate eyebrow positions independently.

Angry expressions should use inward-sloping eyebrows.

Surprised expressions should raise the brows.

Worried expressions should use asymmetric curves.

MOUTH

Create reusable mouth shapes for speech animation.

At minimum, include:

Closed

Small open

Wide open

Rounded

Smile

Frown

Teeth visible
Synchronize mouth changes with the audio when alignment is available.
Do not randomly switch expressions.
Expressions must match the story.
<STEP 7 — BODY ANIMATION>
Animate the characters using proper 2D rigging.
IDLE

Subtle body bobbing

Occasional blinking

Small head movement

Slight hand movement

RUNNING

Alternating arm swings

Coordinated leg movement

Slight torso lean
Body bounce
Footstep synchronization
JUMPING

Anticipation crouch

Upward movement
Legs folding during the jump
Landing squash
Recovery motion
SURPRISE

Rapid head movement

Eyes widening
Arms extending
Body leaning backward
Small recovery bounce
ANGER

Eyebrows lowering

Body leaning forward
Arms raised
Small shaking or impact motion
CELEBRATION
Arms lifting

Body bouncing

Head tilting
Appropriate particle effects
Use spring easing and anticipation.
Never leave a speaking character completely static for several seconds.

Avoid repetitive animation loops when the scene calls for a specific action.

<STEP 8 — BACKGROUNDS>
Create reusable environments inspired by the reference's composition and production quality.
A. BEDROOM
A cartoon bedroom at night.

Include:

Bed with colorful blanket

Bedside table

Lamp

Window

Curtains

Posters

Door

Rug

Warm hallway lighting
Build the room with separate layers.
Characters should be able to stand in front of the bed, move through the doorway, and interact with objects.
B. ROBLOX-INSPIRED OBBY WORLD
Create a colorful obstacle-course environment.
Include:
Floating platforms
Checkpoints
Lava

Clouds

Finish-line signs

Bright geometric obstacles

Stage markers

Allow the avatar to jump across platforms.

Use background depth and perspective to create a sense of scale.
C. GAME SHOP
Create a stylized game-store interface with:
Item panels
Currency counter
Buy buttons
Upgrade icons

Inventory tiles

Progress indicators

The UI should be readable on a phone screen.

D. CARTOON GAME WORLD

Create a larger environment containing:
Grass platforms
Blocky trees
Paths
Decorative buildings
Other avatars

Floating rewards

Particle effects

Design additional environments according to the approved script.

Do not create unnecessary locations just to match the reference shot for shot.
<STEP 9 — GAME INTERFACE DESIGN>
Game-like UI is an important part of the reference.
Create reusable animated interface components.
COUNTDOWN TIMER
Place a rounded dark timer panel near the top center.
Include a stopwatch icon.

Display the relevant time remaining.

At normal time:

Dark background, white text.

At critical time:

Red background, white text.

The timer should animate when the story calls for it.

Treat the timer as a fictional narrative device. It does not need to count down in real time unless the script specifically requires that.

REWARDS

Create pop-up reward graphics such as:

+100 coins

LEVEL UP

NEW POWER

STAGE COMPLETE

LEGENDARY

UNLOCKED

Use animated scale, bounce, and particles.

SHOP INTERFACE

Use:

Dark panels
Rounded corners
Green ownership indicators
Gold currency indicators
Bright purchase buttons
Clear item names

IMPORTANT

The interface must remain crisp and readable.

Use code to render interface typography.

Do not depend on AI-generated images for important numbers or text.
Keep HUD elements consistent between scenes.
<STEP 10 — CAPTIONS>
Captions are a major part of the video's style.
Use large, bold, animated subtitles in the lower-middle portion of the frame.
FONT

Use a heavy rounded sans-serif font such as:

Montserrat ExtraBold

Fredoka Bold

Lilita One

Choose the closest available font after inspecting the reference.

DEFAULT STYLE

Text: White

Outline: Thick black

Shadow: Subtle dark shadow

Alignment: Center

EMPHASIS COLORS

Use:
Green for wins and rewards
Yellow for important objects

Red for danger and urgency

Pink for funny or dramatic words

ANIMATION

Captions should follow the actual spoken dialogue.

Use word-level timestamps.

Display short phrases rather than long paragraphs.

Animate emphasized words with:

Scale pop

Brief overshoot
Small rotation
Bounce
Color change

Keep words on-screen long enough to read.

No caption should cover the main character's face.

Avoid placing captions directly underneath important game buttons.

A caption should typically contain one to five words, depending on timing and screen space.

<STEP 11 — CAMERA MOVEMENT>

Use the camera as part of the storytelling.
CLOSE-UPS
Zoom into the character's face during surprise, anger, or panic.
WIDE SHOTS
Show obstacle courses, larger environments, and groups of characters.

QUICK ZOOMS

Use fast zooms for jokes and sudden reveals.

CAMERA SHAKE

Use very short camera shakes during collisions, explosions, and shocking moments.

TRACKING SHOTS

Follow the avatar during running and jumping sequences.

PARALLAX

Use separated background layers to create depth.

Do not simply zoom into an entire still image.

Move the actual characters and environmental objects.

Use faster camera motion during chaotic moments and slower movement during dialogue.

<STEP 12 — TRANSITIONS>

Use fast, story-driven transitions.

Include:

Hard cuts: For most dialogue and location changes.

Whip pans: For sudden changes or rapid movement.

Zoom transitions: To enter a game world or highlight a discovery.

Impact cuts: For surprising events.

Character wipes: Let a character or object move across the screen to reveal another scene.

Flash frames: Use sparingly for major reveals.

<inputs>
Ask me for my story in one line: who the mean character is, the danger he's in, and the 2-3 people he wronged. If I have no idea, pitch me 3 and let me pick. Length 25-60 s. Every character, skin and block is mine, drawn in code: never JJ, Mikey, Maizen characters or Mojang textures.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1080x1920 30 fps Minecraft-style story Short, built entirely in Blender from code, $0, with no game assets and no AI video.
Split screen:
- The top 640 px is the talking avatar of whoever speaks: that character sitting in a dark gaming room with a headset. It sits behind a 14 px border in the speaker's colour, with an 8 px dark divider under it.
- The bottom 1080x1280 is the block animation.
Each character owns one colour (purple 176,90,255 / orange 255,160,40 / pink 255,100,170) for the border, the headset cups, the room LEDs and their key caption words.
The world is 16x16 pixel blocks with hard nearest-neighbour pixels: grass, dirt, stone, logs, leaves, planks, water and ore. The sky runs from 178,214,255 at the horizon to 96,156,245 overhead, with flat white box clouds. Light comes from a warm sun, using the Standard view transform.
Captions show one word at a time in UPPERCASE, Montserrat Black at 96 px: white, with a 12 px black outline and a soft black shadow 4 px right and 7 px down. Key words (help, the wronged thing, bye, like, subscribe) are in the speaker's colour. The caption sits just under the divider.
Pure dialogue, no narrator. Flashbacks are sepia with a FLASHBACK tag.
Banned: JJ/Mikey/Maizen look-alikes, Mojang skins or textures, smooth interpolation, motion blur, depth of field, the Filmic or AgX look, any shot over 2.5 s, and any frame where nothing moves.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: 25-60 s, about 13 lines per 25 s. Cut every 0.7-2.3 s (median 1.3 s), about 18 shots per 25 s, at least 3 different places.
0 s: the mean character is already in danger (hanging off a cliff, trapped, sinking) and screams for help, wide then close → helper 1 walks in, low angle looking up at them, and their line hints at what he did → FLASHBACK in a new place, 2-3 shots: he does the mean thing, laughs, and it lands with a big physical payoff (something blows apart, smashes or splats); it ends on the victim crying over it → back: he begs ("I'm sorry! I was joking!"), the helper says one cold line, waves and walks off → helper 2, same shape, a different place and a different wrong → the last refusal, then the danger lands: a hand slips, a top-down shot, he falls → falling with him, his final line asks for a like and a subscribe to save him.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools (all free, all local). Install what's missing and tell me what you installed:
   - Blender 4.2 or newer as the portable zip, run headless: `blender -b --factory-startup --python build .py -- MODE OUT [F0 F1]`. Modes: stills, final (F0 F1 re-renders a range), avatars.
   - Python with numpy, Pillow and soundfile.
   - FFmpeg.
   - faster-whisper large-v3-turbo (int8 on the CPU).
   - kokoro-onnx with kokoro-v1.0.onnx and voices-v1.0.bin.
   - Montserrat.
   - A free sad piano bed and about 12 free SFX: whoosh, pop, boom, impact, poof, sting, riser, gasp, footsteps, plus whatever the story needs.
2. Voice (Kokoro, free):
   - Show me the script before recording. Write screams with "!" and keep lines short.
   - Render every line on its own. Trim it at 0.01 amplitude, keeping 10 ms before and 50 ms after.
   - Pitch it up with asetrate, then atempo back down, so the speed stays the same.
   - Kid voices:
     - af_heart, speed 1.14, +1.5 semitones (the main kid)
     - am_echo, speed 1.08, +3 (a boy)
     - af_bella, speed 1.1, +2.5 (a girl)
     - am_puck pitched up sounds bad.
   - Gaps after lines:
     - 0.2-0.45 s normally
     - 0.7-1.2 s where the action needs room (the blast, the slip)
     - 0.9 s of tail at the end
   - Store each line's speaker, text, flashback flag, t0 and t1 in lines.json.
3. Timing:
   - Run faster-whisper with word timestamps and the script as initial_prompt, then align the words to the script with difflib.
   - Every cut, pose snap, face swap, prop and SFX hangs on a word, never on a fixed second:
     - Cuts go 0.06 s before their word.
     - Reaction shots go 0.12 s before a line.
     - Flashbacks start 0.3 s before their first line.
   - Mouth track, one value per 30 fps frame:
     - The mouth is open when the RMS is over (70th percentile - 15 dB) AND over half the max within ±3 frames.
     - Hold every state at least 2 frames.
     - Break any open run longer than 7 frames with 2 closed frames every 6.
4. Textures:
   - Every texture is 16x16, drawn in Pillow. Jitter each pixel ±3-8 so it isn't flat.
   - Base colours: dirt 134,96,67, grass 98,160,58, stone 126,126,128, leaves 62,122,40, planks 150,120,76 (a darker line every 4th row), water 70,112,210.
   - Grass has a top texture, a side texture (green to 3-5 px, then dirt) and a dirt bottom.
   - Every image texture uses Closest interpolation with Extend.
5. World (a voxel mesher):
   - A dict maps (x, y, z) to a block type.
   - Emit one quad only for faces with no neighbour. Water emits only its top face, dropped 0.12.
   - Merge all quads of one texture into one mesh, giving every quad UVs 0..1.
   - Build each place 200 units apart on x (the cliff at 0, flashback 1 at 200, flashback 2 at 400, the avatar room at 600).
   - Split the merged meshes per place with bmesh by face centre. Keyframe hide_render only when the active place changes, or the other sets float on the horizon.
   - Trees: a 4-6 block log with a diamond of leaves. Scatter 1-block flowers. Ore specks go in walls the camera passes.
6. Characters (unit P = 1/16):
   - Body pivot 12P up. Torso 8x4x12P. Head an 8P cube on a neck pivot at the top of the torso.
   - Arms 4x4x12P hang from shoulder pivots at (±6P, 0, 10P). Legs 4x4x12P from hip pivots at (±2P, 0, 0).
   - Every box face gets its own texture:
     - the shirt front (zip, stripe or a pixel heart)
     - sleeves with a skin hand in the bottom 4 px
     - pants with shoes in the bottom 3 px
     - hair on the top and back, hair down to row 6 on the sides
     - long hair as an 8.4x1.6x11P slab behind the head
   - Faces are 16x16 textures on a plane 0.002 in front of the head:
     - Hairline rows 0-3. Eyes 2 px wide at x 3-4 and 11-12, row 7.
     - Eyes: normal (white + iris), wide (2x3 white, for scared), smug (a lid row over half an eye), happy (^ ^), and shut for crying, with light-blue tears (120,190,255) running down to row 14.
     - Brows: 2 px, up, down or sad.
     - Mouths:
       - line (4 px on row 12)
       - smirk, frown, o (2x3)
       - open (4x2 with a red tongue)
       - wail (6x3 with red)
       - laugh (with a white teeth row)
       - grin
     - Every mood gets a closed _c and an open _o face. Build one plane per face and key hide_render per frame, so only one face shows.
   - Poses (degrees, X = forward/back swing, -90 is forward, Y = sideways):
     - walk: 1.9 Hz, legs ±34, arms ±31 against them, bob 0.02·|cos|
     - run: 3.0 Hz, ±55, 10 lean
     - hands on hips: X -6, Y ±24
     - despair: Y ±145, X -20 ± 8 sin(9t)
     - flail: arms up and OUT, X -12 ± 22 sin at 3.1 Hz, Y ±(145 ± 18) at 2.3 Hz, legs ±35 at 3.6 Hz
     - hang: face OUT from the wall, arms at X -198 gripping the edge behind the head, legs kicking ±22 at 2.6 Hz, sway 0.9 Hz
     - wave: the arm to X -160, swinging ±18 at 3 Hz
     - shove: arms -80 to -95 with a 14 lean, back ease over 0.14 s
     - turn and leave: rotate over 0.22-0.25 s, then walk out
     - Talkers nod their neck. Listeners look up or down at the speaker with neck angles of 20-30.
7. Animation and FX:
   - Write the whole film as one frame(t) function. Key every object every frame, then set ALL fcurve keys to CONSTANT, so it snaps like the real thing.
   - Fuse block: pops in with a back ease over 0.15 s. A white overlay box flashes, speeding up from 3 to 12 Hz until the blast.
   - Blast:
     - Build the target from loose blocks. Each launches away from the blast at 5-9 × max(0.45, 1.4 - dist/9) sideways and 4-8 up, spins ±9 rad/s, falls at gravity 20 and stops where it lands.
     - 22 smoke cubes (two thirds white with a little glow, a third grey) grow to 1.9 in 0.35 s, drift 1.4-3.4 out and shrink away after 0.45 s.
     - A 9000 W orange point light decays as e^(-7t).
     - Camera shake: 0.22·e^(-3.2t).
     - Cut to the ruin with a few loose blocks lying around.
   - Splat: 26 cubes of 0.13 (3 white : 1 red) fly out at 1.5-3.5 with gravity 9, shrinking after 0.6 s. Swap the victim to a face with splats painted on.
   - Party props: balloons bob 0.12 at 1.9 Hz on strings, plus boxes with ribbons. Candle flames glow at emission 6.
   - Fall: z = -0.5·13·t². The falling shot orbits at 2.9 units, from -28° to +22° over 3.6 s, dropping with him. Add a 260 W fill light that follows the camera in dark shafts.
8. Shots and light:
   - Vertical sensor fit (fov is vertical):
     - closes at 40-44
     - mediums at 46-52
     - wides at 56
     - a low angle at 44 looking up at whoever refuses
   - Every shot pushes 0.2-0.5 units with smoothstep. Shake = (sin 61t, cos 47t, sin 53t) × 0.01 on panicky closes.
   - Put the camera perpendicular to the line between two characters.
   - Light:
     - Sun 3.2, angle 1.5°, colour 1.0,0.96,0.9, lighting the side the camera sees.
     - World strength 0.6.
     - Clouds: flat boxes 4-8 × 3-6 × 1 at height 34, emission 0.4.
   - Render Eevee with ray tracing and shadows, 40 samples, at 1080x1280. Stills: 16 samples at 50%, 3 frames per shot (start, middle, end). Look at them before any full render.
9. Avatar strip:
   - A dark room: wall 34,30,52, shelves with coloured boxes and a black chair.
   - A 60 W blue-white area light as the monitor.
   - A headset built from boxes, its cups in the speaker's colour (emission 1.5).
   - 3 LED strips in the speaker's colour (emission 8) and a 120 W rim light in that colour.
   - Sun 0.15, world 0.2.
   - The character sits chest-up, arms slightly forward, camera at fov 34.
   - Render every face of every character as a 1080x640 still (avatars mode).
10. Edit (Pillow + FFmpeg):
   - Canvas 14,12,20.
   - Avatar:
     - Pick the avatar from the current speaker, their mood for that line, and the mouth track.
     - Zoom it 1.10 and let it breathe 1.2% at sin(2.2t).
     - Pop it on every speaker change: 1 - 0.05·e^(-14Δ)·cos(22Δ).
   - Captions:
     - Each word appears 0.03 s early, pops in as 1 + 0.18·e^(-18Δ), and stays until the next word, at most 0.9 s.
     - Strip punctuation.
   - Flashbacks:
     - The grade is 75% sepia (g·1.07+0.06, g·0.93+0.03, g·0.72) mixed with 25% of the original, plus a 45% vignette.
     - A white flash at each edge: e^(-22|t-edge|), capped at 0.95.
     - A 40 px FLASHBACK tag in the bottom right.
   - Sound:
     - Voice median at -15 dB.
     - Piano bed at -29 dB RMS, dipped to 55% inside flashbacks with 0.25 s smoothing.
     - One SFX per event, trimmed to its hit:
       - boom at -10
       - splat at -15
       - sting on the first slip at -17
       - riser on the fall at -20
       - pops at -20 to -26
       - a whoosh 0.15 s before every flashback edge at -22
       - impacts at -22
       - footsteps at -30
       - a gasp at -28
     - Mix to -14 LUFS with a tanh soft clip at 0.89.
   - Encode H.264 (slow, CRF 18, yuv420p) with AAC at 192k.
</build>

<gotchas>
- Blender colours must be 0-1 and linear. If you pass 0-255 values, the sky renders thousands of times too bright and every frame goes white.
- Folded arms, or arms raised forward, cover a block face from front and low angles. Use hips, or arms up and OUT.
- A character hanging off a ledge must face out, or you only ever see the back of his head.
- Objects built from boxes all sit at location 0. Sort them into places by their mesh's vertex centre, after view_layer.update().
- Set hide_render, then keyframe it on every frame, or old keys win and the faces never switch.
- Keep cameras out of tree leaves, and keep clouds out of the sky right behind a head, or they read as a hat.
- Kokoro gives 24 kHz audio with no word times. Resample it to 48 kHz and take the timings from faster-whisper.
- A full render is about 1.6 s a frame. Do the stills pass first and re-render only the frame ranges that changed.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my story (or pitch me 3), show me the script, then render the stills pass before the full video.
</start>

Tilt .26 rad, spin .55 degrees per second. Day/night uses smoothstep(-.12, .24, N·L) with the light direction recomputed from Sun to Earth every frame. Navy night side with ~380 warm city lights, a coral band on the terminator, a cyan rim, ocean specular, an atmosphere halo that is stronger on the lit side.
A small astronaut mascot (~180px) built from rounded rectangles: suit #f3f7fb, orange #ff8f4a boots, a visor gradient #1f5a73 to #0a1c2c with glowing cyan eyes that look at whatever matters, a blinking antenna light, an idle bob, squash and stretch on every pose.
Type: Fredoka 600/700 only. Captions in caps with 3-6px letter spacing in teal #8fd8e6, gold #ffd98a or white, sitting in rounded pills of rgb(6,20,40) at 62%. Every line of text rises 1.3x its own height through a clip on an ease-out-quint.
Finish: a vignette to rgba(4,4,20,.45) and a 6% film grain re-randomized 24 times per second.
Banned: outlines, flares or loops on the Sun's edge, static infographic strips, full stops in on-screen text, text that fades in whole, AI images or AI video, Kurzgesagt's own characters, bird or music.
</direction>

<structure>
30 seconds, every line of narration gets a camera move or a transformation, nothing ever holds still.
Tight on the Sun at 2.25x (0s) → on the word "vanished" it swells 6% for 0.22s, collapses in 0.33s, then a white flash and a shockwave ring (1s) → pull back to 1x revealing Earth still lit and the astronaut staring at the empty spot (1.6-3s) → on "eight" an 8:20 countdown slams in from 1.7x to 1x and starts ticking, a "LAST LIGHT" label rides the edge of the growing dark disc (3.2s) → dive to 2.3x on Earth with light streaks flowing in (5.6s) → on "you" a YOU pin drops (7s) → on "left" a photon lands on the pin with "THIS LIGHT LEFT THE SUN / 8 MIN 20 SEC AGO" (7.5s) → on "play" the pin morphs into a play button, "YOU PRESSED PLAY / 15 SEC AGO" (8.8s) → one pull-back from 2.4x to a 0.3x orbit view, "LAST LIGHT" and "GRAVITY" riding the ring (9.6-12.5s) → on "nothing" a dotted circle at the empty centre (13.4s) → on "hits" the darkness sweeps Earth in 0.7s, city lights pop on, the countdown turns gold at 0:00 (15.8s) → on "black" the background fades almost to black (17.4s) → Jupiter appears, "STILL SHINING FOR 1 HOUR+" (17.9s) → zoom out, a dashed tangent line, "30 KM/S" as Earth flies straight off (20.8s) → a thermometer counts 15 to -70°C while frost grows from the poles (22.8s) → a 0.8s rewind on a separate story clock (24.3s) → sunglasses drop onto the astronaut (25.2s) → a photon tagged "8:20 OLD", then the title (27.7s).
For any other topic, keep the same shape: the event happens on its word, pull back to show scale, dive in to make it personal ("you"), pull back out, the consequence with a live counter, an escalation, a funny beat with the mascot, a callback and the title.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file. Every frame is a pure function of time: http://window.seek(t) draws frame t. No timers, no CSS animation.
2. Camera moves on easeInOutCubic, zoom is interpolated in log space, every pop is a damped spring (damping .42-.5, frequency 12-16).
3. Voice: ElevenLabs eleven_v4 with a designed voice (calm, warm, curious male, late 30s, crisp, light neutral European English), stability .5, similarity .75, generated with timestamps. Without a key, use kokoro-onnx locally and get word times with faster-whisper. Every animation event fires on its word. About 165 words per minute, 0.24s between sentences, a 0.36s beat before the big reveal.
4. The darkness front: any pixel within the front's radius from the Sun turns to night with a 30px soft edge. The front moves at ~47px/s and ramps to 700px/s near Earth.
5. Keep two clocks: ambient time for twinkle, spin and bob, and a separate story clock for events, so a rewind stays consistent.
6. Render with Playwright in headless Edge with the GPU: seek every frame at 30fps and blend 2 subframes (shutter 0.6) for motion blur, then encode with libx264 at CRF 16 for the master and CRF 20 for delivery.
7. Sound: a calm royalty-free space music bed 7dB under the voice, timed so its natural ending lands on the title, swelling 5dB under the title. One downloaded royalty-free sound effect per event kind (collapse, impact, pull-back whoosh, countdown tick, dive, pin tap, photon land, play click, light hit, reveal, frost, rewind), each peak-aligned to its frame and 4-10dB under the voice. Master with gain plus a limiter to -14 LUFS, -2.2dB true peak.
</build>

<gotchas>
Make the WebGL globe canvas at least 2 x radius x zoom x 1.18 pixels or the sphere clips flat in close-ups. Never draw prominences on the Sun's edge, they read as white hooks. Never pad the voice to fit the visuals, tighten the read instead. Speed the darkness front up near Earth or it takes 13 seconds to cross the planet. Show me a contact sheet of every beat before rendering.
</gotchas>

<inputs>
Ask me for: my story in one line (someone does something strange, plus the real reason behind it, which is the twist) and the length (45-60 s). If I have no idea, pitch me 3 stories with their twists and let me pick. Every story is mine, never a copy of an existing video.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1080x1920 30 fps Short that looks like a premium 3D cartoon, built entirely in code with three.js and rendered frame by frame in headless Chrome. No AI images or video, no stock 3D models.
- Characters: big-headed toon people. A sphere head sits straight on a rounded bean torso (no neck), mitten hands, simple legs, clothes as flat painted panels (collars, pockets, ties), white matte skin.
- Faces are drawn live on the head every frame from about 100 numbers (eye openness and lid shape, pupils, brow height, angle and curve, mouth width, opening, smile and corners, teeth, tongue, blush) in ink #2A1D17, never swapped pictures. Make at least 20 named expressions (neutral, bored, smug, skeptical, shocked, scared, starstruck with star eyes, sad, angry, whistle...) as presets that morph: brows lead, the mouth trails, 2 frames of anticipation, 10% overshoot, settle. Shock squeezes for 2 frames, then pops.
- Talking: whoever speaks a quoted line moves their mouth from the voice loudness inside each word's timestamps, with the shape from the letters (wide A, round O and U, lips shut on M, B and P, teeth together on S, F and T). Silent characters keep still mouths.
- World: the whole film is ONE connected map built once. Every location sits at its own spot (doors lead to rooms, the street is outside the front door), densely dressed: 15+ props in every wide, three depth layers, signs and screens with real text on them. Every shot is a camera placed somewhere in that world, so shots match and people stay where they were. Hero props are 1.5-2.5x real size with 3+ parts you can name.
- Light: a warm key, a cool fill, a warm rim on every silhouette, contact shadows and ambient occlusion so nothing floats. Saturated colour, never washed out. Bloom 0.3, vignette 0.28, light grain, slight sharpen.
- Numbers are objects: every number the narrator says appears on a real thing (a screen, a counter, a sign, a cheque) and rolls up on its word.
- Captions: two words at a time, Montserrat ExtraBold about 100 px, white with a thick black outline, centred at 70% of the height, stepping clear of faces.
- A fast, casual adult narrator in third person, deadpan, with the dialogue lines acted on screen.
Banned: AI video, stock models, floating labels, arrows, stickers or HUDs (text only on real objects), motion blur, depth of field, any shot that holds still, things that pop in or vanish (everything is carried, thrown or slides in), hands through objects, and the narrator saying sound words.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: 45-60 s at about 230 wpm. About 2.6 edits per 10 s (2.1-3.9), a median shot of about 2.5 s, and never two edits under 0.4 s apart: the camera carries two beats in one shot instead of cutting.
0 s: the strangest act in one line, already happening in frame 0 → the setup in 2-3 lines with the stakes on screen → escalation, every line bigger than the last, dialogue acted by the character who says it → "You see,": the real explanation as its own staged scene (a cutaway, a dream, a model of the thing) → the twist, the real reason, shown not said → the payoff picture lands on the last word and holds 1 s.
Joins: 77% are 6-frame dissolves with both cameras still moving; about 1 in 9 is a zoom-through (push into a door, a screen or an eye and land in the next shot); hard cuts under 5%; one whip per film at most.
Camera: it moves in 86% of frames. A push-in is the default (about x1.28 over 1.35 s, its fastest frame on a word). Pull-out reveals start fast and land soft, then pans and trucks; cranes and orbits are rare. A slow creep between beats, still moving into every edit, never parked.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools. Everything is free and local except the voice. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed:
   - Node 20, three.js (pin the version), puppeteer with headless Chrome and the GPU on
   - Python with numpy, plus FFmpeg
   - faster-whisper with large-v3-turbo, int8 on the CPU
   - an ElevenLabs API key (ask me for it, and never print it)
   - the Montserrat font
   - free sounds from Pixabay or Mixkit: whooshes, pops, impacts, door, bell, footsteps, crowd murmur, one room tone per place
2. Voice: write about 24 short lines per 55 s and show me the script before you record. Ask before spending credits. Make one ElevenLabs take with eleven_multilingual_v2 and a premade casual male voice, all lines in one request. Tighten silences over 0.25 s down to 0.12 s. Never change the narrator's pitch.
3. Timing: run faster-whisper with word timestamps on the final voice and match it to the script with difflib. Key every cut, face change, gesture and SFX to a word index, never to a fixed second.
4. Engine: one page that draws any time t (frames are pure functions of time: no http://Date.now, seeded random only). Each shot is build(S) with its clause; it reuses the cached world and only places the camera and the actors. Render every shot to an offscreen target; a dissolve mixes two targets. Draw captions on a 2D canvas on top.
5. Animation: every action has 2-6 frames of anticipation, the action on its word, 5-15% overshoot and a settle. Holds stay still but alive (blinks every 1.5-4 s, small eye darts). Verbs: walk along paths through doors, reach, take, hold, throw with a wind-up and a ballistic arc, catch, put into with the container opening and closing, dig, show (hold it up to the lens), shrug, point, slam, double take. A prop only moves when a hand moves it.
6. Shots: eye-level 3/4 by default, low for power, high for small or caught, top-down inserts for hands on props, over the shoulder, profile two-shots, one dutch at most. The same subject twice in a row gets a new angle or size. The key object fills 0.45-0.7 of the frame width, and faces sit above the caption band. Before the full render, make one 50% still per shot and look at every one.
7. Edit and sound: voice median at -15 dB; an SFX on every visible action (a whoosh on camera moves, an impact on contact); room tone per place at -30 dB; an optional music bed at -24 dB ducking under words. Mix to -14 LUFS. Encode H.264 (CRF 17, yuv420p) with AAC at 256k.
</build>

<gotchas>
Set renderer.outputColorSpace and every colour texture's colorSpace to SRGBColorSpace, or everything renders washed out. Use preserveDrawingBuffer and wait for fonts and textures before the first capture, or the first frames come out blank. Build the world once and reuse geometry and materials; rebuilding every frame makes the render crawl. Dissolves ghost big faces, so frame one side of every dissolve medium or wider. Arms go through heads and bodies unless you push hand targets out of the torso and head. Whisper merges short words, so find real silences in the audio and give each word gap the longest silence near it. Render stills first, then re-render only the shots that changed.
</gotchas>
